```{r}
#| echo: false
#| include: false
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setup: libraries and the helpers used throughout the deck.
# (Hidden — the plotting helpers of Lectures 6-9 plus this lecture's
#  unit-root helpers, as in the lecture notebook.)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(gridExtra)
  library(urca)        # ur.df, ur.pp, ur.kpss, ur.ers, ur.za, punitroot (Pfaff 2008)
})

# Time-series line plot; optional dashed reference line at the mean.
ts_plot <- function(x, mu = NULL, title = NULL) {
  time_idx <- if (is.ts(x)) as.numeric(time(x)) else seq_along(x)
  df <- data.frame(time = time_idx, value = as.numeric(x))
  p <- ggplot(df, aes(time, value)) +
    theme_classic() + geom_line() + labs(x = "Time", y = NULL, title = title)
  if (!is.null(mu)) p <- p + geom_hline(yintercept = mu, linetype = "dashed")
  p
}

# Sample ACF with approximate +/- 2/sqrt(T) bands (lag 0 dropped).
sample_acf_plot <- function(x, L = 20, title = NULL, by = 3) {
  a  <- acf(x, plot = FALSE, lag.max = L)
  df <- data.frame(lag = as.numeric(a$lag)[-1], acf = as.numeric(a$acf)[-1])
  b  <- 2 / sqrt(length(x))
  ggplot(df, aes(lag, acf)) + theme_classic() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, y = 0, yend = acf), linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(b, -b), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, L, by = by)) +
    labs(x = "Lag", y = "Sample ACF", title = title)
}

# Sample PACF with the same bands.
sample_pacf_plot <- function(x, L = 20, title = NULL, by = 3) {
  a  <- pacf(x, plot = FALSE, lag.max = L)
  df <- data.frame(lag = as.numeric(a$lag), acf = as.numeric(a$acf))
  b  <- 2 / sqrt(length(x))
  ggplot(df, aes(lag, acf)) + theme_classic() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, y = 0, yend = acf), linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(b, -b), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, L, by = by)) +
    labs(x = "Lag", y = "Sample PACF", title = title)
}

# Theoretical impulse response = Wold coefficients psi_0 = 1, psi_1, psi_2, ...
irf_plot <- function(ar = numeric(0), ma = numeric(0), h = 20, title = NULL) {
  psi <- c(1, ARMAtoMA(ar = ar, ma = ma, lag.max = h))
  df  <- data.frame(horizon = 0:h, response = psi)
  ggplot(df, aes(horizon, response)) + theme_classic() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = horizon, y = 0, yend = response)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, h, by = 4)) +
    labs(x = "Horizon after a unit innovation", y = "Response", title = title)
}

# Roots of a lag polynomial with the unit circle; roots ON the circle are blue.
roots_plot <- function(roots, title = NULL, tol = 1e-6) {
  theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 400)
  circ  <- data.frame(x = cos(theta), y = sin(theta))
  where <- ifelse(abs(Mod(roots) - 1) < tol, "on the circle",
                  ifelse(Mod(roots) > 1, "outside", "inside"))
  df    <- data.frame(Real = Re(roots), Imaginary = Im(roots), where = where)
  ggplot() + theme_classic() +
    geom_path(data = circ, aes(x, y), colour = "grey55") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
    geom_point(data = df, aes(Real, Imaginary, colour = where), size = 3) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(outside = "black", inside = "red",
                                   `on the circle` = "blue"), name = NULL) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(x = "Real part", y = "Imaginary part", title = title)
}

# A series and its sample ACF side by side: the first two pictures to look at.
ts_acf_panel <- function(x, title = NULL, L = 20, mu = NULL) {
  grid.arrange(ts_plot(x, mu = mu, title = title),
               sample_acf_plot(x, L = L, title = "Sample ACF"), ncol = 2)
}

# A series with its fitted OLS trend line (red, dashed).
with_trend <- function(y, title) {
  tt  <- seq_along(y)
  fit <- lm(y ~ tt)
  ts_plot(y, title = title) +
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(fit)[1], slope = coef(fit)[2],
                colour = "red", linetype = "dashed")
}

# How often a series crosses its fitted OLS trend line.
crossings <- function(y) {
  tt <- seq_along(y)
  sum(diff(sign(residuals(lm(y ~ tt)))) != 0)
}

# (Augmented) Dickey-Fuller test with urca::ur.df(), reported the way we read it:
# the test regression, each statistic against its 5% critical value, and for tau
# the MacKinnon (1996) p-value for the actual number of observations.
df_report <- function(y, type = c("none", "drift", "trend"), lags = 0,
                      selectlags = c("Fixed", "AIC", "BIC"), label = NULL) {
  type <- match.arg(type); selectlags <- match.arg(selectlags)
  fit  <- ur.df(as.numeric(y), type = type, lags = lags, selectlags = selectlags)
  co   <- summary(fit)@testreg$coefficients[, 1:3, drop = FALSE]
  rn   <- sub("^z.diff.lag$", "z.diff.lag1", rownames(co))
  rn   <- sub("^z.diff.lag(\\d+)$", "alpha\\1", rn)
  rn[rn == "(Intercept)"] <- "c"; rn[rn == "z.lag.1"] <- "gamma"; rn[rn == "tt"] <- "delta (trend)"
  rownames(co) <- rn
  id   <- colnames(fit@teststat); stat <- fit@teststat[1, ]; cv5 <- fit@cval[, "5pct"]
  left <- startsWith(id, "tau"); nobs <- length(fit@res)
  pval <- rep(NA_real_, length(id))
  pval[left] <- punitroot(stat[left], N = nobs,
                          trend = c(none = "nc", drift = "c", trend = "ct")[[type]])
  tests <- data.frame(
    statistic = round(as.numeric(stat), 3), cv_5pct = as.numeric(cv5),
    p_value   = round(pval, 4),
    H0 = c(tau1 = "gamma = 0", tau2 = "gamma = 0", tau3 = "gamma = 0",
           phi1 = "c = gamma = 0", phi2 = "c = delta = gamma = 0",
           phi3 = "delta = gamma = 0")[id],
    decision = ifelse(ifelse(left, stat < cv5, stat > cv5), "reject H0", "do not reject"),
    row.names = c(tau1 = "tau", tau2 = "tau_mu", tau3 = "tau_tau",
                  phi1 = "Phi1", phi2 = "Phi2", phi3 = "Phi3")[id])
  cat(sprintf("%sDF regression: type = \"%s\", %d lagged difference(s), %d observations\n",
              if (is.null(label)) "" else paste0(label, " - "), type,
              sum(startsWith(rn, "alpha")), nobs))
  print(signif(co, 4)); cat("\n"); print(tests)
  invisible(list(fit = fit, coef = co, tests = tests))
}

# Fast DF t-ratio (no lagged differences) for Monte Carlo loops.
df_tau <- function(y, type = c("none", "drift", "trend")) {
  type <- match.arg(type)
  dy <- diff(y); ylag <- head(y, -1); n <- length(dy)
  X  <- switch(type, none  = cbind(ylag),
                     drift = cbind(1, ylag),
                     trend = cbind(1, seq_len(n), ylag))
  XtXi <- solve(crossprod(X)); b <- XtXi %*% crossprod(X, dy)
  k  <- ncol(X); s2 <- sum((dy - X %*% b)^2) / (n - k)
  b[k] / sqrt(s2 * XtXi[k, k])
}

# Fast ADF t-ratio with p chosen by AIC/BIC over 0..pmax on a common sample.
adf_tau <- function(y, type = c("drift", "none", "trend"), pmax = 0,
                    ic = c("BIC", "AIC", "fixed")) {
  type <- match.arg(type); ic <- match.arg(ic)
  dy <- diff(y); n <- length(dy); rows <- (pmax + 1):n; m <- length(rows)
  X0 <- switch(type, none  = cbind(y[rows]),
                     drift = cbind(1, y[rows]),
                     trend = cbind(1, rows, y[rows]))
  L  <- matrix(0, m, pmax); for (j in seq_len(pmax)) L[, j] <- dy[rows - j]
  fit_p <- function(p) {
    X <- cbind(X0, L[, seq_len(p), drop = FALSE])
    XtXi <- solve(crossprod(X)); b <- XtXi %*% crossprod(X, dy[rows])
    rss <- sum((dy[rows] - X %*% b)^2); k <- ncol(X); g <- ncol(X0)
    list(ic  = m * log(rss / m) + k * (if (ic == "AIC") 2 else log(m)),
         tau = b[g] / sqrt(rss / (m - k) * XtXi[g, g]))
  }
  fits <- lapply(0:pmax, fit_p)
  best <- if (ic == "fixed") pmax + 1 else which.min(sapply(fits, `[[`, "ic"))
  c(tau = fits[[best]]$tau, p = best - 1)
}

# Confirmatory analysis: ADF (BIC lags), Phillips-Perron and KPSS with 5% c.v.s.
confirm <- function(y, trend) {
  pmax <- floor(12 * (length(y) / 100)^0.25)
  a <- ur.df(y, type = if (trend) "trend" else "drift", lags = pmax, selectlags = "BIC")
  p <- ur.pp(y, type = "Z-tau", model = if (trend) "trend" else "constant", lags = "short")
  k <- ur.kpss(y, type = if (trend) "tau" else "mu", lags = "short")
  c(ADF = a@teststat[1], `ADF 5%` = a@cval[1, "5pct"],
    PP  = p@teststat[1], `PP 5%`  = p@cval[1, "5pct"],
    KPSS = k@teststat[1], `KPSS 5%` = k@cval[1, "5pct"])
}

# Consecutive integers as "start-end" strings (for date-stamping bubbles).
runs <- function(k) {
  if (!length(k)) return("none")
  s <- split(k, cumsum(c(1, diff(k) != 1)))
  paste(sapply(s, function(r) paste(range(r), collapse = "-")), collapse = ", ")
}

# Confirmatory battery for a real series: PP, KPSS, DF-GLS and Zivot-Andrews.
battery <- function(y, trend, p) {
  pp <- ur.pp(y, type = "Z-tau", model = if (trend) "trend" else "constant", lags = "short")
  kp <- ur.kpss(y, type = if (trend) "tau" else "mu", lags = "short")
  gl <- ur.ers(y, type = "DF-GLS", model = if (trend) "trend" else "constant", lag.max = p)
  za <- ur.za(y, model = if (trend) "both" else "intercept", lag = p)
  stat <- c(pp@teststat, kp@teststat, gl@teststat, za@teststat)
  cv   <- c(pp@cval[1, "5pct"], kp@cval[1, "5pct"], gl@cval[1, "5pct"], za@cval[2])
  rej  <- c(stat[1] < cv[1], stat[2] > cv[2], stat[3:4] < cv[3:4])
  out  <- data.frame(H0 = c("unit root", "stationary", "unit root", "unit root, no break"),
                     statistic = round(as.numeric(stat), 3), cv_5pct = round(as.numeric(cv), 3),
                     decision = ifelse(rej, "reject H0", "do not reject"),
                     row.names = c("Phillips-Perron Z_tau", "KPSS", sprintf("DF-GLS (%d lags)", p),
                                   sprintf("Zivot-Andrews (model %s)", if (trend) "C" else "A")))
  print(out)
  cat("Zivot-Andrews: last year before the break =", time(y)[za@bpoint], "\n")
  invisible(za)
}
```

## The tools: **urca** {.smaller}

| Function | Test |
|:---|:---|
| `ur.df()` | Dickey–Fuller and augmented DF, with $\Phi$ statistics |
| `ur.pp()` | Phillips–Perron |
| `ur.kpss()` | KPSS stationarity test |
| `ur.ers()` | ERS DF-GLS and point-optimal |
| `ur.za()` | Zivot–Andrews with an endogenous break |
| `punitroot()` | MacKinnon (1996) $p$-values for DF statistics |
| `df_report()`, `df_tau()` | *our helpers*: readable (A)DF output; fast DF $t$-ratio |

::: {.callout-ts}
`ur.df(y, type = "none"/"drift"/"trend", lags, selectlags)`: with `"AIC"/"BIC"`, `lags` is the **maximum** and zero lags is never selected. Critical values come from the next tabulated $T$ **above** yours — in borderline cases read the MacKinnon $p$-value. `tseries::adf.test()` always includes constant **and** trend.
:::

# Trends and random walks {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## Deterministic versus stochastic trends {.smaller}

A **deterministic trend** plus a stationary disturbance is a **trend-stationary (TS)** process
$$
Y_t=\mu+\delta t+u_t,\qquad u_t\ \text{a stationary ARMA process}.
$$
Shocks are **temporary**: $Y_t$ keeps returning to the line $\mu+\delta t$; **detrending** leaves a stationary series.

A **stochastic trend** accumulates past shocks — canonically, the random walk with drift
$$
\Delta Y_t=\delta+\varepsilon_t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Y_t=Y_0+\delta t+\sum_{i=1}^{t}\varepsilon_i ,
$$
in which every innovation is **permanent** — it enters every future $Y_{t+h}$ with weight one.

::: {.keybox}
$Y_t$ is not stationary but $\Delta Y_t$ is: a **difference-stationary (DS)** process. More generally, DS means $\Delta Y_t=\delta+u_t$ with $u_t$ stationary.
:::



## Predict: a trend-stationary series vs a random walk {.smaller}

We draw, with $T=500$:

- a **TS** series: $\mu=0.8$, $\delta=0.2$, AR(1) noise with $\phi=0.8$;
- a **random walk** with the same drift $\delta=0.2$;

and plot each with its fitted OLS trend line. We also count how often each crosses its fitted trend.

> **Predict:**
>
> 1. Which series keeps returning to its trend line?
> 2. Which one could stay on one side of it for a hundred periods?
> 3. Which will cross its fitted trend more often — and by roughly how much?


## R — TS series vs random walk {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
set.seed(123)
T  <- 500; tt <- 1:T
y_ts <- 0.8 + 0.2 * tt + as.numeric(arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.8), n = T))   # TS
y_ds <- cumsum(0.2 + rnorm(T))                                                 # DS

cat("Crossings of the fitted trend line:  TS =", crossings(y_ts),
    "   DS =", crossings(y_ds), "\n")
grid.arrange(with_trend(y_ts, "Trend-stationary: 0.8 + 0.2t + AR(1)"),
             with_trend(y_ds, "Random walk with drift 0.2"), ncol = 2)
```

## Reading the graphs {.smaller}

- The **TS series** hugs its trend line and crosses it **105** times in 500 periods. With $\phi=0.8$ a shock has a half-life of about three periods; the series is pulled back to the line.
- The **random walk** crosses its fitted trend only **28** times and spends stretches of a hundred periods or more on one side — nothing pulls it back, every shock is permanent.

::: {.keybox}
The fitted line is itself **misleading** for the random walk: its intercept and slope are estimated from a series that has no tendency to return to *any* line.
:::

> Same drift, same average slope — completely different behaviour around the trend.

## The pure random walk {.smaller}

$Y_t=Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$, i.e. $\Delta Y_t=\varepsilon_t$, $\varepsilon_t\sim\text{i.i.d.}(0,\sigma^2)$. Conditional on a fixed $Y_0$:
$$
E(Y_t)=Y_0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)=t\sigma^2,\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t-j})=(t-j)\sigma^2 .
$$
The mean is constant but the variance grows without bound — **not stationary**. The correlation depends on $t$:
$$
\rho_{j,t}=\frac{(t-j)\sigma^2}{\sqrt{t\sigma^2\,(t-j)\sigma^2}}=\sqrt{\frac{t-j}{t}} .
$$

::: {.keybox}
For fixed $j$, $\rho_{j,t}\to1$ as $t$ grows; for fixed $t$ it falls only slowly in $j$. This is the **correlogram signature of a unit root**: sample autocorrelations that start near one and decline roughly **linearly**, not geometrically.
:::

::: {.small .muted}
The *sample* ACF decays a little faster (it is computed around the sample mean), but the slow decay is unmistakable.
:::

## The random walk with drift {.smaller}

Adding a constant, $\Delta Y_t=\delta+\varepsilon_t$, gives
$$
Y_t=Y_0+\delta t+\sum_{i=1}^{t}\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
E(Y_t)=Y_0+\delta t,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)=t\sigma^2 .
$$

::: {.keybox}
A nonzero constant in the **differences** produces a **deterministic trend in the level**, while the persistence remains stochastic.
:::

> This is why the constant plays a **different role in each Dickey–Fuller regression** — keep it in mind for the testing strategy.

## Random walk plus noise {.smaller}

Add measurement error $\eta_t\sim\text{WN}(0,\sigma^2_\eta)$, independent of $\varepsilon_t$ — the **local-level model**:
$$
Y_t=Y_0+\sum_{i=1}^{t}\varepsilon_i+\eta_t,
\qquad
\Delta Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\eta_t-\eta_{t-1}.
$$
$\operatorname{Var}(Y_t-Y_0)=t\sigma^2+\sigma^2_\eta$, covariances $(t-j)\sigma^2$: correlations slightly below the pure random walk's. $\Delta Y_t$ is an **MA(1)** with $\rho_1=-\sigma^2_\eta/(\sigma^2+2\sigma^2_\eta)\in(-\tfrac12,0]$: its coefficient is **negative** and approaches $-1$ as $\sigma^2_\eta/\sigma^2$ grows.

::: {.callout-ts}
The MA root nearly **cancels** the unit AR root: the series looks almost stationary — exactly where unit-root tests break down.
:::

> **Beveridge–Nelson (1981):** *every* $I(1)$ process = random walk (permanent) + stationary process (transitory).

## Predict: 2000 random walks {.smaller}

We draw 2000 random walks of length $T=200$ starting from zero, with $\sigma^2=1$, and plot the first 50.

> **Predict:**
>
> 1. What **shape** should the band containing about 95% of the paths have?
> 2. What should the cross-sectional variance be at $t=50$, $100$ and $200$?
> 3. What will the **sample ACF of a single path** look like?

## R — the spread of random walks {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 100%
set.seed(123)
T <- 200
paths <- replicate(2000, cumsum(rnorm(T)))                    # T x 2000 matrix
cat("Cross-sectional variance at t = 50, 100, 200:",
    round(apply(paths[c(50, 100, 200), ], 1, var), 1), "  (theory: 50, 100, 200)\n")
cat("Share of paths outside +/- 2 sqrt(t) at t = 200:",
    round(mean(abs(paths[200, ]) > 2 * sqrt(200)), 3), "\n")

df  <- data.frame(time = rep(1:T, 50), value = as.vector(paths[, 1:50]),
                  path = rep(1:50, each = T))
env <- data.frame(time = 1:T, hi = 2 * sqrt(1:T), lo = -2 * sqrt(1:T))
g_paths <- ggplot(df, aes(time, value, group = path)) + theme_classic() +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = env, aes(time, hi), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = env, aes(time, lo), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = NULL, title = "50 random walks with +/- 2 sqrt(t) band")

p_acf <- sample_acf_plot(paths[, 1], L = 20, title = "Sample ACF of the first path")

grid.arrange(g_paths, p_acf, ncol = 2)
```

## What you should see {.smaller}

- The cross-sectional variances (**46.8, 88.6, 191.3**) are close to $t\sigma^2=50,100,200$: the spread of possible paths grows like $\sqrt t$ — a **parabola-shaped** band.
- **4.1%** of paths lie outside $\pm2\sqrt t$ at $t=200$, close to the 4.6% implied by the normal distribution.
- Each individual path seems to have trends and cycles — **none of which is real**.
- The sample ACF of a single path starts at about **0.93** and declines almost linearly, still **0.23** at lag 20.

::: {.keybox}
Slow, near-linear ACF decay is the **unit-root signature** — quite unlike the geometric decay of a stationary AR(1).
:::

# Unit roots and integration {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## The unit root {.smaller}

AR($p$): $\phi(L)Y_t=c+\varepsilon_t$, $\phi(z)=1-\phi_1z-\cdots-\phi_pz^p$. Stationary when all roots of $\phi(z)=0$ lie **outside** the unit circle. 

A **unit root** is a root at $z=1$:
$$
\phi(1)=1-\phi_1-\phi_2-\cdots-\phi_p=0 .
$$
For an AR(1) this is $\phi=1$: the random walk. (A root at $z=-1$ also lies on the circle but generates an oscillation at frequency $\pi$ — a seasonal-type unit root; here "unit root" means $z=1$.)

## Factoring out the unit root {.smaller}

**AR(2) example.** With inverse roots $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, $\phi(L)=(1-\lambda_1L)(1-\lambda_2L)$; one unit root when $\lambda_1=1$, $|\lambda_2|<1$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_t=1.5Y_{t-1}-0.5Y_{t-2}+\varepsilon_t
&\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
(1-L)(1-0.5L)Y_t=\varepsilon_t\\
&\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
(1-0.5L)\Delta Y_t=\varepsilon_t .
\end{aligned}
$$
Roots: $z=1$ (on the circle) and $z=2$ (outside). A **double** unit root, $(1-L)^2Y_t=\varepsilon_t$, must be differenced twice.

::: {.keybox}
A single unit root factors as $\phi(L)=(1-L)\phi^\ast(L)$, with $\phi^\ast$ of order $p-1$ and stationary, so
$\Delta Y_t=c+\phi^\ast_1\Delta Y_{t-1}+\cdots+\phi^\ast_{p-1}\Delta Y_{t-p+1}+\varepsilon_t$ is a stationary AR($p-1$) **in the differences**.
:::

## Shocks become permanent {.smaller}

Write the differences in Wold form, $\Delta Y_t=\delta+\psi^\ast(L)\varepsilon_t$ with $\psi^\ast(L)=\beta(L)/\phi^\ast(L)$. The response of the **level** is the **cumulated** response of the difference:
$$
\frac{\partial Y_{t+h}}{\partial\varepsilon_t}=\sum_{j=0}^{h}\psi^\ast_j
\;\longrightarrow\;
\psi^\ast(1)=\frac{\beta(1)}{\phi^\ast(1)}\qquad(h\to\infty).
$$

::: {.keybox}
$\psi^\ast(1)$ is the **long-run impact** of a shock — Campbell and Mankiw (1987) use it to measure the persistence of output fluctuations. For the AR(2) above, $\psi^\ast(1)=1/(1-0.5)=2$: a unit shock eventually raises $Y$ by **two** units, permanently.
:::

$$\boxed{\text{stationary: }\lim_{h\to\infty}\partial Y_{t+h}/\partial\varepsilon_t=0},\qquad
\boxed{\text{unit root: }\lim_{h\to\infty}\partial Y_{t+h}/\partial\varepsilon_t=\psi^\ast(1)\neq0}.$$

## Integration and ARIMA models {.smaller}

A process that must be differenced $d$ times to become stationary (and invertible) is **integrated of order $d$**, $Y_t\sim I(d)$. Stationary series are $I(0)$; random walks are $I(1)$.

If $\Delta^dY_t$ is a stationary ARMA($p,q$), $Y_t$ is an **ARIMA($p,d,q$)** process:
$$
\phi(L)(1-L)^dY_t=c+\beta(L)\varepsilon_t .
$$
ARIMA(1,1,0) is $\Delta Y_t=c+\phi\Delta Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ — the AR(2) example with $c=0$ and $\phi=0.5$.

::: {.callout-ts}
In R, `arima(y, order = c(p, d, q))` differences internally, but with $d\ge1$ it **drops the constant**. Add a drift as a regressor (`xreg = seq_along(y)`) or fit the model to `diff(y)`.
:::

## Predict: roots and impulse responses {.smaller}

Compare two AR(2) processes:

| | $\phi_1$ | $\phi_2$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Stationary AR(2) of Lectures 6–9 (model A) | $0.5$ | $0.25$ |
| Unit-root AR(2), $(1-L)(1-0.5L)$ | $1.5$ | $-0.5$ |

> **Predict:**
>
> 1. Where do the roots of each lag polynomial lie relative to the unit circle?
> 2. What does each **impulse response** converge to as the horizon grows?

## R — roots and impulse responses {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: "80%"
ar_stat <- c(0.5, 0.25)    # Lectures 6-9, model A
ar_unit <- c(1.5, -0.5)    # (1 - L)(1 - 0.5L)
cat("Moduli of the roots, stationary AR(2):", round(Mod(polyroot(c(1, -ar_stat))), 3), "\n")
cat("Moduli of the roots, unit-root  AR(2):", round(Mod(polyroot(c(1, -ar_unit))), 3), "\n")
cat("Response after 40 periods:  stationary =", signif(ARMAtoMA(ar = ar_stat, lag.max = 40)[40], 3),
    "   unit root =", round(ARMAtoMA(ar = ar_unit, lag.max = 40)[40], 4), "\n")
grid.arrange(
  roots_plot(polyroot(c(1, -ar_stat)), title = "Roots: phi = (0.5, 0.25)"),
  roots_plot(polyroot(c(1, -ar_unit)), title = "Roots: phi = (1.5, -0.5)"),
  irf_plot(ar = ar_stat, h = 20, title = "Impulse response: stationary"),
  irf_plot(ar = ar_unit, h = 20, title = "Impulse response: unit root") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red"),
  ncol = 2)
```

## Reading the graphs {.smaller}

- **Stationary AR(2):** both roots outside the unit circle (moduli 1.24 and 3.24); the impulse response is essentially zero after 40 periods ($1.5\times10^{-4}$).
- **Unit-root AR(2):** one root exactly **on** the circle (blue), one at $z=2$. The impulse response rises from 1 to 1.5, 1.75, … and converges to $\psi^\ast(1)=2$ (dashed red line).

::: {.keybox}
A shock to a unit-root process is **never undone**. With a stationary $\phi^\ast(L)$ the level adjusts gradually — but to a permanently **different** value.
:::

## $I(0)$ versus $I(1)$: a summary {.smaller}

| Property | $I(0)$ | $I(1)$ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Variance | finite and constant | grows with $t$ |
| Autocorrelations | decay quickly; $\sum_j\lvert\rho_j\rvert<\infty$ | stay close to one, decay slowly |
| Effect of a shock | transitory | permanent |
| Mean reversion | frequent crossings of the mean | expected time between crossings is infinite |
| Long-horizon forecast | converges to the mean (or trend) | the current level plus drift |
| Forecast-error variance | bounded | grows linearly with the horizon |

## One model that nests the cases {.smaller}

The **component form** $Y_t=\mu+\delta t+u_t$, $u_t=\phi u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$, nests TS and DS. Substituting $u_t=Y_t-\mu-\delta t$ into the AR(1) gives the reduced form
$$
\boxed{\;Y_t=\underbrace{\mu(1-\phi)+\phi\delta}_{\text{constant}}\;+\;\underbrace{\delta(1-\phi)}_{\text{trend coefficient}}\,t\;+\;\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t .\;}
$$

- $|\phi|<1$: **trend-stationary** ($\delta\neq0$) or stationary around $\mu$ ($\delta=0$).
- $\phi=1$: the trend coefficient **vanishes** and the constant becomes $\delta$, so $\Delta Y_t=\delta+\varepsilon_t$ — a random walk with drift (pure random walk if $\delta=0$).

::: {.keybox}
Under the unit-root null the deterministic terms are **restricted** — so the $\Phi$ tests test them **jointly** with $\phi=1$.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
eps = {
  // seeded uniform (mulberry32) + Box-Muller: same shocks for a given draw
  let s = (draw * 2654435761) >>> 0;
  const rnd = () => {
    s = (s + 0x6D2B79F5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(s ^ (s >>> 15), 1 | s);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
  const out = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
    const u1 = rnd() || 1e-12, u2 = rnd();
    out.push(Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u1)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * u2));
  }
  return out;
}
sim = {
  const n = 200, delta = 0.2;
  let u = 0; const y = [];
  for (let t = 1; t <= n; t++) { u = phi * u + eps[t - 1]; y.push({t: t, y: delta * t + u}); }
  const mt = (n + 1) / 2, my = d3.mean(y, d => d.y);
  let sxy = 0, sxx = 0;
  for (const d of y) { sxy += (d.t - mt) * (d.y - my); sxx += (d.t - mt) ** 2; }
  const b = sxy / sxx, a = my - b * mt;
  let cross = 0, prev = null;
  for (const d of y) {
    const sg = Math.sign(d.y - (a + b * d.t));
    if (prev !== null && sg !== prev) cross++;
    prev = sg;
  }
  return {y: y, a: a, b: b, cross: cross,
          fit: [{t: 1, y: a + b}, {t: n, y: a + b * n}]};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 225, marginLeft: 45,
  x: {label: "t"},
  y: {label: "Y_t", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(sim.y, {x: "t", y: "y", stroke: "#1b3a6b", strokeWidth: 1.4}),
    Plot.line(sim.fit, {x: "t", y: "y", stroke: "#c0392b", strokeDasharray: "6,4", strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})
```

    &nbsp;·&nbsp; reduced form: constant φδ = <b>${(phi * 0.2).toFixed(3)}</b>,
    trend coefficient δ(1−φ) = <b>${(0.2 * (1 - phi)).toFixed(3)}</b>
  </div>
</div>`

Push $\phi$ to 1: crossings collapse and the reduced-form **trend coefficient vanishes**, yet the level still trends — now via the drift through the unit root.
:::

## Detrend or difference? {.smaller}

**Stochastic** trend → **difference**; **deterministic** trend → **detrend**. The wrong choice is costly in **both** directions.

**Over-differencing a TS series.** If $Y_t=\mu+\delta t+\varepsilon_t$, then $\Delta Y_t=\delta+\varepsilon_t-\varepsilon_{t-1}$: an MA(1) with coefficient $-1$, a **unit root in the MA polynomial**. Stationary but **not invertible**; $\rho_1=-0.5$ and the PACF decays slowly. Differencing a stationary AR(1) gives the ARMA(1,1) $\Delta Y_t=\phi\Delta Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t-\varepsilon_{t-1}$: needless structure that hurts identification and forecasts.

**Detrending a DS series.** Regressing a random walk on time does **not** remove its stochastic trend. The residuals remain $I(1)$ and show long spurious "cycles" (Nelson and Kang 1981).

::: {.callout-ts}
Any business-cycle measure obtained by linearly detrending a series with a stochastic trend is **suspect**.
:::

## Predict: the wrong transformation {.smaller}

Two experiments with $T=500$ and the **same** shocks:

1. a TS series with white-noise errors, $Y_t=0.8+0.2t+\varepsilon_t$;
2. a random walk with drift 0.5.

Each is both **differenced** and **detrended**.

> **Predict:**
>
> 1. What will the sample ACF of $\Delta y_t$ show at lag 1 for the TS series? What will its PACF look like?
> 2. What will the ACF of the **detrended** TS series look like?
> 3. For the random walk, what will the ACFs of the differenced and of the detrended series look like?

## R — over-differencing a TS series {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: "90%"
set.seed(123)
T  <- 500; tt <- 1:T
y7   <- 0.8 + 0.2 * tt + rnorm(T)
dy7  <- diff(y7)                       # over-differenced: MA(1) with coefficient -1
d1y7 <- residuals(lm(y7 ~ tt))         # detrended: white noise
cat("Lag-1 sample autocorrelation:  differenced =", round(acf(dy7, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], 3),
    "   detrended =", round(acf(d1y7, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], 3), "\n")
grid.arrange(ts_plot(dy7, mu = 0.2, title = "TS series: first difference"),
             sample_acf_plot(dy7,  L = 12, title = "ACF of the difference"),
             sample_pacf_plot(dy7, L = 12, title = "PACF of the difference"),
             ts_plot(d1y7, mu = 0, title = "TS series: detrended"),
             sample_acf_plot(d1y7,  L = 12, title = "ACF of the detrended series"),
             sample_pacf_plot(d1y7, L = 12, title = "PACF of the detrended series"),
             ncol = 3)
```

## R — detrending a random walk {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: "80%"
set.seed(123)
y5 <- e <- rnorm(T)
for (t in 2:T) y5[t] <- 0.5 + y5[t - 1] + e[t]
dy5  <- diff(y5)                       # white noise with mean 0.5
d1y5 <- residuals(lm(y5 ~ tt))         # still I(1)
cat("Lag-1 sample autocorrelation:  differenced =", round(acf(dy5, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], 3),
    "   detrended =", round(acf(d1y5, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], 3), "\n")
cat("Crossings of zero by the detrended series:", sum(diff(sign(d1y5)) != 0), "in", T, "periods\n")
grid.arrange(ts_plot(dy5, mu = 0.5, title = "RW with drift: first difference"),
             sample_acf_plot(dy5, L = 12, title = "ACF of the difference"),
             ts_plot(d1y5, mu = 0, title = "RW with drift: detrended"),
             sample_acf_plot(d1y5, L = 12, title = "ACF of the detrended series"),
             ncol = 2)
```

## Interpretation {.smaller}

**Trend-stationary series.**

- The first difference has lag-1 autocorrelation **$-0.499$** — the $-0.5$ of a non-invertible MA(1) — and nothing significant beyond. Its PACF is negative and decays slowly ($-0.50,\,-0.37,\,-0.23,\dots$): the fingerprint of an MA root **on** the unit circle. Differencing would lead a modeller to an MA(1) with $\hat\beta\approx-1$.
- The detrended series is white noise (lag 12 just crosses — the kind of isolated long lag Lecture 9 warned us not to chase).

> Differencing a TS series manufactures an MA unit root.

## Interpretation, continued {.smaller}

**Random walk with drift.**

- The first difference is white noise around 0.5 (lag-1 autocorrelation $-0.055$).
- The detrended series is **not**: lag-1 autocorrelation **0.963**, slow ACF decay, only **28** zero-crossings in 500 periods — long swings that look like business cycles but are an **artefact** of detrending a stochastic trend.

$$\boxed{\text{difference a TS series}\Rightarrow\text{MA unit root}}$$
$$\boxed{\text{detrend a DS series}\Rightarrow\text{spurious cycles}}$$

::: {.small .muted}
Both experiments use the same shocks, so the differenced random walk and the detrended TS series have identical correlograms: each is just the original white noise.
:::

# Why the $t$-test fails under a unit root {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## OLS when $\phi=1$ {.smaller}

Take $Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$, $Y_0=0$, and
$$
\hat\phi=\frac{\sum_{t=2}^{T}Y_tY_{t-1}}{\sum_{t=2}^{T}Y_{t-1}^2}.
$$
When $|\phi|<1$, Lecture 9 gave $\sqrt T(\hat\phi-\phi)\overset{d}{\to}N(0,\,1-\phi^2)$. At $\phi=1$ that variance is **zero** — a first hint that something changes.

Because $\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)=t\sigma^2$, the denominator grows like $T^2$, not $T$, and (Phillips 1987)
$$
T(\hat\phi-1)\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{\tfrac12\{W(1)^2-1\}}{\int_0^1W(r)^2\,dr},
\qquad
\tau=\frac{\hat\phi-1}{\operatorname{SE}(\hat\phi)}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{\tfrac12\{W(1)^2-1\}}{\big\{\int_0^1W(r)^2\,dr\big\}^{1/2}},
$$
where $W(r)$ is a standard **Brownian motion**, the continuous-time limit of a scaled random walk.

## Four consequences {.smaller}

1. **Superconsistency.** $\hat\phi$ converges at rate $T$, not $\sqrt T$.
2. **Non-normal, skewed limits.** $W(1)^2\sim\chi^2(1)$ and $P\{\chi^2(1)<1\}\approx0.68$, so about **two-thirds** of estimates fall **below** one even though $\phi=1$. OLS is biased downwards, and $\tau$ lies to the **left** of $N(0,1)$.
3. **Deterministic terms matter.** A constant (or trend) replaces $W$ by demeaned (detrended) Brownian motion: the distribution moves **further left**; each case needs its own critical values.
4. **Simulated critical values.** No closed form: Dickey and Fuller (1979) and Fuller (1976) tabulated them; MacKinnon (1996) response surfaces give them, and $p$-values, for any $T$.



## Predict: the Dickey–Fuller distributions {.smaller}

We simulate **20,000** random walks with $T=100$ and compute $\tau$ from three regressions:

- no deterministic terms;
- a constant;
- a constant and a trend.

> **Predict:**
>
> 1. Where will the 5% quantiles lie relative to the normal value $-1.645$?
> 2. In what order will the three distributions line up?
> 3. If you used $-1.645$ with the **trend** regression, how often would you wrongly reject a true unit root?

## R — $\tau$ under a unit root {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(123)
R <- 20000; T <- 100
sims <- t(replicate(R, {
  y  <- cumsum(rnorm(T))
  yl <- head(y, -1)
  c(none = df_tau(y, "none"), constant = df_tau(y, "drift"), trend = df_tau(y, "trend"),
    phi_hat = sum(yl * y[-1]) / sum(yl^2))
}))
cat("Quantiles of tau under H0   (N(0,1): 1% -2.33, 5% -1.645, 10% -1.28)\n")
print(round(apply(sims[, 1:3], 2, quantile, c(0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50)), 2))
cat(sprintf("\nShare of phi_hat below 1: %.3f      Mean of phi_hat: %.4f\n",
            mean(sims[, "phi_hat"] < 1), mean(sims[, "phi_hat"])))
cat(sprintf("Rejection rate of a TRUE unit root using -1.645 with the trend regression: %.3f\n",
            mean(sims[, "trend"] < -1.645)))
```

## R — the three densities {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: "90%"
dens <- data.frame(tau = as.vector(sims[, 1:3]),
                   regression = factor(rep(c("none", "constant", "constant + trend"), each = R),
                                       levels = c("none", "constant", "constant + trend")))
ggplot(dens, aes(tau, linetype = regression)) + theme_classic() +
  geom_density(key_glyph = "path") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, colour = "red", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1.645, colour = "red", linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = expression(tau), y = "Density", linetype = NULL,
       title = "Dickey-Fuller distributions under a unit root (T = 100); N(0,1) in red")
```

## Reading the output {.smaller}

- The simulated 5% points are **$-1.97$, $-2.90$, $-3.47$** — reproducing the Dickey–Fuller tables for $T=100$ ($-1.95$, $-2.89$, $-3.45$).
- All lie well to the left of $-1.645$, and **each deterministic term moves the distribution further left**.
- **68.0%** of the $\hat\phi$ fall below one, as $P\{\chi^2(1)<1\}=0.68$ predicts; their mean is 0.982, not 1.

::: {.keybox}
Using the normal critical value with the trend regression would reject a **true** unit root in **77%** of samples.
:::

> Under a unit root, "$t<-1.645$" is not evidence of anything.

# Dickey–Fuller tests and a testing strategy {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## The Dickey–Fuller regressions {.smaller}

Subtract $Y_{t-1}$: $\Delta Y_t=\gamma Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$, $\gamma=\phi-1$; test $H_0:\gamma=0$ vs $H_1:\gamma<0$. The $t$-ratio $\hat\gamma/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\gamma)$ (identical to $(\hat\phi-1)/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\phi)$) is compared with **Dickey–Fuller**, not normal, critical values.
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{none:}  && \Delta Y_t=\gamma Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\\
&\text{drift:} && \Delta Y_t=c+\gamma Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\\
&\text{trend:} && \Delta Y_t=c+\delta t+\gamma Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t
\end{aligned}
$$
Dickey and Fuller (1981) add $F$-type statistics for **joint** hypotheses on deterministic terms and $\gamma$:
$$
\Phi=\frac{(\text{RSS}_R-\text{RSS}_U)/r}{\text{RSS}_U/(T-k)},
$$
with $r$ restrictions and $k$ parameters in the unrestricted regression.

## The statistics and their critical values {.smaller}

| Regression | $H_0$ | Statistic (urca name) | 5% c.v., $T=100$ | 5% c.v., $T=500$ |
|:---|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|
| trend | $\gamma=0$ | $\tau_\tau$ (`tau3`) | $-3.45$ | $-3.42$ |
| | $\delta=\gamma=0$ | $\Phi_3$ (`phi3`) | $6.49$ | $6.30$ |
| | $c=\delta=\gamma=0$ | $\Phi_2$ (`phi2`) | $4.88$ | $4.71$ |
| drift | $\gamma=0$ | $\tau_\mu$ (`tau2`) | $-2.89$ | $-2.87$ |
| | $c=\gamma=0$ | $\Phi_1$ (`phi1`) | $4.71$ | $4.61$ |
| none | $\gamma=0$ | $\tau$ (`tau1`) | $-1.95$ | $-1.95$ |

> Compare the one-sided 5% normal value, $-1.645$: the $\tau$ critical values are much more negative, and move further left as deterministic terms are added.

::: {.callout-ts}
The $\Phi$ statistics look like ordinary $F$ statistics but have **non-standard** distributions and their own critical values.
:::

## Choosing the deterministic terms {.smaller}

Think about $H_1$ as well as $H_0$ — both should fit what the data could be (Hamilton 1994, §17.4; Elder and Kennedy 2001).

| Regression | Under $H_0$ ($\gamma=0$) | Under $H_1$ ($\gamma<0$) | Use when the data… |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| none | RW without drift | zero-mean stationary AR | fluctuate around zero |
| drift | RW without drift ($c=0$) | stationary, nonzero mean | no trend, nonzero level |
| trend | RW with drift | trend-stationary | trend |

::: {.keybox}
- **Omitting a term that is present makes the test inconsistent**: a TS series tested with the drift regression almost never rejects, however large $T$.
- **Including a term that is absent costs power**: each extra term moves the critical value left.
:::

> For a trending series, **start with the trend regression** — under the alternative only it describes the data.

## The augmented Dickey–Fuller test {.smaller}

Autocorrelated errors invalidate the DF distribution. Any AR($p$) can be written
$$
\Delta Y_t=c+\gamma Y_{t-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\alpha_i\,\Delta Y_{t-i}+\varepsilon_t,
\qquad
\gamma=-\phi(1)=\phi_1+\cdots+\phi_p-1,
\qquad
\alpha_i=-\sum_{j=i+1}^{p}\phi_j ,
$$
— a unit root is again $\gamma=0$. E.g. for an AR(3):
$$
\Delta Y_t=(\phi_1+\phi_2+\phi_3-1)Y_{t-1}-(\phi_2+\phi_3)\Delta Y_{t-1}-\phi_3\Delta Y_{t-2}+\varepsilon_t .
$$
The **ADF** regression adds lagged differences to the chosen deterministic terms:
$$
\Delta Y_t=c+\delta t+\gamma Y_{t-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_i\,\Delta Y_{t-i}+\varepsilon_t .
$$

## ADF critical values and the lag length {.smaller}

> $\tau$ and $\Phi$ keep **the same** critical values. With ARMA errors, ADF stays valid if $p$ grows with $T$, no faster than $T^{1/3}$ (Said and Dickey 1984).

**Choosing $p$.**

- Set a maximum, e.g. Schwert's (1989) rule $p_{\max}=\lfloor12(T/100)^{1/4}\rfloor$.
- Go **general-to-specific** — drop the last lag while insignificant (Ng and Perron 1995) — or minimize **AIC/BIC** over $p\le p_{\max}$ on a common sample.
- Check the residuals are white noise (Ljung–Box, Lecture 9).

::: {.callout-ts}
Too few lags leave autocorrelation and **distort the size**; too many waste degrees of freedom and **reduce power**.
:::

## More than one unit root {.smaller}

If $I(2)$ is possible, test **from the top down** (Dickey and Pantula 1987): first test for a unit root in $\Delta Y_t$,
$$
\Delta^2Y_t=c+\gamma\,\Delta Y_{t-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_i\,\Delta^2Y_{t-i}+\varepsilon_t ,
$$
and only if that is rejected test $Y_t$ itself.

::: {.keybox}
**Top-down** (Dickey and Pantula 1987): testing $Y_t$ first assumes there is at most one unit root.
:::

> $I(2)$ is rare in economics; nominal price levels and money stocks are sometimes candidates.

## The sequential procedure (1/2) {.smaller}

The true deterministic terms are unknown, and both omitting and including them have costs. Start from the most general plausible model and simplify only when the data allow (Dolado, Jenkinson and Sosvilla-Rivero 1990; Enders 2015, Ch. 4):

1. **Trend regression.** Estimate $\Delta Y_t=c+\delta t+\gamma Y_{t-1}+\sum\alpha_i\Delta Y_{t-i}+\varepsilon_t$; test $\gamma=0$ with $\tau_\tau$. **Rejected** → $Y_t$ is (trend-)stationary: stop; ordinary $t$-tests on $c$, $\delta$ are now valid.
2. **Is the trend needed?** If $\tau_\tau$ does not reject, test $\delta=\gamma=0$ with $\Phi_3$. If $\Phi_3$ rejects, the trend belongs: test $\gamma=0$ again with the **standard normal** (with a trend in the DGP the $t$-ratio is asymptotically normal; West 1988). Still not rejected → unit root with a trend in the differences: stop.
3. **Drift regression.** If $\Phi_3$ does not reject, drop the trend and test with $\tau_\mu$. Rejects → stationary around a mean: stop.

## The sequential procedure (2/2) {.smaller}

4. **Is the drift needed?** If $\tau_\mu$ does not reject, test $c=\gamma=0$ with $\Phi_1$. If $\Phi_1$ rejects, the drift belongs: test $\gamma=0$ with the standard normal. Non-rejection → random walk with drift: stop.
5. **No deterministic terms.** If $\Phi_1$ does not reject, estimate $\Delta Y_t=\gamma Y_{t-1}+\cdots$ and test with $\tau$. Non-rejection → random walk without drift.
6. **Confirm the order of integration** by testing $\Delta Y_t$ the same way. Rejecting a unit root in $\Delta Y_t$ confirms $Y_t\sim I(1)$.

::: {.keybox}
You rarely need every step: a plot, and economic knowledge — *does the series grow?* — can replace a low-powered pre-test (Elder and Kennedy 2001).
:::

> Knowing **why** each step is there — what the series looks like under $H_0$ and $H_1$ — matters more than following the chart.

## Six data generating processes {.smaller}

$T=500$. $Y_1$–$Y_3$ share one set of AR(1) shocks, $Y_4$–$Y_6$ another: within each group, differences come **only** from the deterministic terms and the unit root.

| Series | Simulated as | Implied DF regression | Class |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| $Y_1$ | $Y_t=0.8Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ | $\Delta Y_t=-0.2Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ | $I(0)$, mean 0 |
| $Y_2$ | $Y_t=2+u_t$, $u_t=0.8u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ | $\Delta Y_t=0.4-0.2Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ | $I(0)$, mean 2 |
| $Y_3$ | $Y_t=0.8+0.2t+u_t$ | $\Delta Y_t=0.32+0.04t-0.2Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ | trend-stationary |
| $Y_4$ | $Y_t=Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ | $\Delta Y_t=\varepsilon_t$ | $I(1)$, pure random walk |
| $Y_5$ | $Y_t=0.5+Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ | $\Delta Y_t=0.5+\varepsilon_t$ | $I(1)$ with drift |
| $Y_6$ | $Y_t=0.5+0.2t+Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ | $\Delta Y_t=0.5+0.2t+\varepsilon_t$ | $I(1)$; $\Delta Y_t$ trend-stationary |

> **Predict:** from the plots that follow, which DF regression would you **start** with for each series, and which do you expect to **reject** the unit root?

## R — the six series {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: "80%"
T  <- 500; tt <- 1:T
set.seed(123); y1 <- as.numeric(arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.8), n = T))
set.seed(123); y2 <- 2 + as.numeric(arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.8), n = T))
set.seed(123); y3 <- 0.8 + 0.2 * tt + as.numeric(arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.8), n = T))
set.seed(123); e  <- rnorm(T)
y4 <- y5 <- y6 <- e
for (t in 2:T) {
  y4[t] <- y4[t - 1] + e[t]                        # pure random walk
  y5[t] <- 0.5 + y5[t - 1] + e[t]                  # random walk with drift
  y6[t] <- 0.5 + 0.2 * t + y6[t - 1] + e[t]        # random walk, drift and trend
}
grid.arrange(ts_plot(y1, mu = 0, title = "Y1: AR(1)"),
             ts_plot(y2, mu = 2, title = "Y2: AR(1) with mean 2"),
             ts_plot(y3, title = "Y3: AR(1) around a linear trend"),
             ts_plot(y4, title = "Y4: pure random walk"),
             ts_plot(y5, title = "Y5: random walk with drift"),
             ts_plot(y6, title = "Y6: random walk with drift and trend"), ncol = 2)
```

## R — their correlograms {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: "80%"
grid.arrange(sample_acf_plot(y1, title = "Sample ACF: Y1"), sample_acf_plot(y2, title = "Sample ACF: Y2"),
             sample_acf_plot(y3, title = "Sample ACF: Y3"), sample_acf_plot(y4, title = "Sample ACF: Y4"),
             sample_acf_plot(y5, title = "Sample ACF: Y5"), sample_acf_plot(y6, title = "Sample ACF: Y6"),
             ncol = 2)
```

## Reading the graphs {.smaller}

- $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ are the same series shifted by 2: both fluctuate around a fixed level, cross it often, and have geometrically decaying ACFs.
- $Y_3$ and $Y_5$ both rise steadily and **look much alike** — yet one is trend-stationary and the other a random walk with drift. Both ACFs decay slowly.
- $Y_4$ wanders with no tendency to return anywhere.
- $Y_6$ curves upwards — its level grows **quadratically** — and its ACF also decays slowly.

::: {.keybox}
The correlograms separate $Y_1$, $Y_2$ from the rest but **cannot** separate a deterministic from a stochastic trend. That is the job of the tests.
:::

## Case 1: three stationary series {.smaller}

The plots suggest **none** for $Y_1$ (fluctuates around zero), **drift** for $Y_2$ (nonzero level, no trend) and **trend** for $Y_3$. No lags: the series are AR(1).

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
r1 <- df_report(y1, type = "none",  label = "Y1"); cat("\n")
r2 <- df_report(y2, type = "drift", label = "Y2"); cat("\n")
r3 <- df_report(y3, type = "trend", label = "Y3")
cat(sprintf("\nImplied mean of Y2,  -c/gamma          = %.2f   (true 2)\n",
            -r2$coef["c", 1] / r2$coef["gamma", 1]))
cat(sprintf("Implied slope of Y3, -delta/gamma      = %.3f  (true 0.2)\n",
            -r3$coef["delta (trend)", 1] / r3$coef["gamma", 1]))
```

## Case 1: reading the output {.smaller}

- **$Y_1$.** $\hat\gamma=-0.26$, so $\hat\phi=0.74$. $\tau=-8.71\ll-1.95$: reject. $Y_1$ is $I(0)$, with neither a deterministic nor a stochastic trend.
- **$Y_2$.** $\tau_\mu=-8.77<-2.87$: reject. Because $Y_2$ is $I(0)$, the ordinary $t$-ratio on the constant (7.41) is **valid**; $\Phi_1$ is irrelevant once the unit root is rejected. Implied mean $-\hat c/\hat\gamma=2.16$ (true 2).
- **$Y_3$.** $\tau_\tau=-8.76<-3.42$: reject; the trend's ordinary $t$-ratio (8.75) is valid — trend-stationary. The trend coefficient 0.053 is **not** the slope but $\delta(1-\phi)$; dividing by $-\hat\gamma$ recovers the slope, **0.200**.

::: {.keybox}
The three estimates of $\gamma$ are almost identical ($-0.263$, $-0.266$, $-0.266$): the series share shocks, and **correctly specified deterministic terms leave the estimate of persistence unchanged**.
:::

## Case 2: a pure random walk ($Y_4$) {.smaller}

$Y_4$ shows no trend. Pretending we don't know how it was generated, it could be a random walk or a stationary series with a nonzero mean — so start with **drift**; if the drift is unnecessary, re-test without it; finally test the difference.

> **Predict:** which of $\tau_\mu$, $\Phi_1$, $\tau$ and the test on $\Delta Y_4$ will reject?

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
r4  <- df_report(y4, type = "drift", label = "Y4"); cat("\n")
r4a <- df_report(y4, type = "none",  label = "Y4"); cat("\n")
r4b <- df_report(diff(y4), type = "none", label = "diff(Y4)")
```

## Case 2: reading the output {.smaller}

1. $\tau_\mu=-1.60>-2.87$ (MacKinnon $p=0.48$): cannot reject a unit root.
2. Step 4: is the constant needed? $\Phi_1=1.62<4.61$: $c=\gamma=0$ not rejected — the drift regression is **over-parameterized**.
3. Re-test without the constant: $\tau=-0.60>-1.95$ — still a unit root, now with the **more powerful** test.
4. $\Delta Y_4$ rejects decisively ($\tau=-23.5$, $\hat\gamma=-1.05$: $\Delta Y_4$ is white noise).

::: {.callout-ts}
The constant's $t$-ratio of 1.70 tells us **nothing** here: under a unit root it does not have a $t$ distribution. Use $\Phi_1$.
:::

> $Y_4\sim I(1)$: a pure random walk.

## Case 3: a random walk with drift ($Y_5$) {.smaller}

$Y_5$ trends, so start with the **trend** regression: under the alternative only a trend-stationary model could describe it.

> **Predict:** will $\tau_\tau$ reject? Will the trend survive $\Phi_3$? Is there a drift?

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
r5  <- df_report(y5, type = "trend", label = "Y5"); cat("\n")
r5a <- df_report(y5, type = "drift", label = "Y5"); cat("\n")
cat("Regression of diff(Y5) on a constant (valid: diff(Y5) is stationary):\n")
print(round(summary(lm(diff(y5) ~ 1))$coefficients, 4))
```

## Case 3: reading the output {.smaller}

- **Trend regression.** $\tau_\tau=-2.57>-3.42$ ($p=0.30$): do not reject. The trend's $t$-ratio, 2.59, *looks* significant but that inference is invalid under a unit root. The right test: $\Phi_3=3.48<6.30$ — the trend is **not** needed. ($\Phi_2=53.2$ rejects $c=\delta=\gamma=0$: some deterministic term is present — pointing to a drift.)
- **Drift regression.** $\tau_\mu=0.48$: no evidence against the unit root. $\Phi_1=75.6>4.61$ rejects $c=\gamma=0$: the drift belongs. Step 4: compare the $t$-ratio on $\gamma$ with the **normal** — at 0.48, still nowhere near significant.
- **Confirming the drift.** $\Delta Y_5$ is stationary, so regressing it on a constant is ordinary: mean **0.536** (s.e. 0.044), close to the true 0.5.

::: {.keybox}
$Y_5$ is $I(1)$ with drift. The linear trend in its graph comes from the **drift accumulating through the unit root**, not from a deterministic trend — exactly the distinction the TS/DS debate is about.
:::

## Case 4: drift and trend ($Y_6$) {.smaller}

$Y_6$ curves upwards: a unit root combined with a trend in the differences gives a **quadratic** trend in the level.

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| results: hold
r6  <- df_report(y6, type = "trend", label = "Y6"); cat("\n")
dy6 <- diff(y6)
cat("Regression of diff(Y6) on a constant and trend (index 1 = period 2):\n")
print(round(summary(lm(dy6 ~ seq_along(dy6)))$coefficients, 4)); cat("\n")
r6b <- df_report(dy6, type = "trend", label = "diff(Y6)")
```

## R — the first difference of $Y_6$ {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
ts_acf_panel(dy6, title = "First difference of Y6")
```

## Case 4: reading the output {.smaller}

- $\tau_\tau=0.74$: no evidence against the unit root ($\hat\gamma\approx2\times10^{-5}$).
- $\Phi_3$ is **enormous**: $\delta=\gamma=0$ rejected, the trend is needed; the $t$-ratio on $\gamma$ (0.74) compared with the normal still does not reject.
- Regressing $\Delta Y_6$ on a constant and trend: slope **0.2002** (true 0.2), intercept 0.69 (true $0.5+0.2=0.7$, because the index starts at period 2). The DF trend test on $\Delta Y_6$ rejects decisively ($\tau_\tau=-23.5$).

::: {.keybox}
$Y_6$ is $I(1)$ with **both** a stochastic trend and a deterministic trend in its differences — hence the quadratic level. $\Delta Y_6$'s sample ACF decays slowly only because of its linear trend; once detrended it is white noise.
:::

## Summary of the six cases {.smaller}

| Series | Start with | Path through the procedure | Conclusion |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| $Y_1$ | none | $\tau$ rejects | $I(0)$, zero mean |
| $Y_2$ | drift | $\tau_\mu$ rejects | $I(0)$, nonzero mean |
| $Y_3$ | trend | $\tau_\tau$ rejects | trend-stationary |
| $Y_4$ | drift | $\tau_\mu$, $\Phi_1$ ✗ → none: $\tau$ ✗; $\Delta Y_4$ ✓ | $I(1)$, no drift |
| $Y_5$ | trend | $\tau_\tau$, $\Phi_3$ ✗ → drift: $\tau_\mu$ ✗, $\Phi_1$ ✓; mean of $\Delta Y_5$ significant | $I(1)$ with drift |
| $Y_6$ | trend | $\tau_\tau$ ✗, $\Phi_3$ ✓; $\gamma=0$ ✗ (normal); $\Delta Y_6$ trend-stationary | $I(1)$, trend in differences |

::: {.small .muted}
✓ rejects $H_0$ · ✗ does not reject. **Caution:** these series are long and generated by exactly the models the tests assume; real series — shorter, with breaks, volatility shifts or MA components — are rarely this clear.
:::

# Confirmatory tests, size and power {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## Phillips–Perron {.smaller}

ADF handles serial correlation **parametrically** (add lags). Phillips and Perron (1988) estimate the **non-augmented** DF regression and correct its $t$-ratio **non-parametrically**:
$$
Z_\tau=\frac{\hat\sigma}{\hat\lambda}\,\tau-\frac{\hat\lambda^2-\hat\sigma^2}{2\hat\lambda}\cdot\frac{T\,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\gamma)}{s},
$$
$\hat\sigma^2$ the residual variance, $s$ the regression standard error, $\hat\lambda^2$ a Newey–West estimate of the **long-run variance** $\lambda^2=\sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty}\gamma_j$. With white-noise errors $\lambda^2=\sigma^2$ and $Z_\tau=\tau$.

::: {.keybox}
Under $H_0$, $Z_\tau$ has the same limit as $\tau$ for the same deterministic terms: **the DF critical values apply**. PP is robust to general serial correlation and heteroskedasticity.
:::

::: {.callout-ts}
PP is **badly over-sized** when the errors have a large **negative** MA root (Schwert 1989) — see the size experiment below.
:::

## KPSS: reversing the hypotheses {.smaller}

Kwiatkowski, Phillips, Schmidt and Shin (1992):
$$
Y_t=\delta t+r_t+u_t,\qquad r_t=r_{t-1}+\eta_t,\qquad \eta_t\sim\text{WN}(0,\sigma^2_\eta),
$$
$u_t$ stationary. $H_0:\sigma^2_\eta=0$ — $r_t$ is a constant and $Y_t$ is **stationary** around a level ($\delta=0$) or a trend. If $\sigma^2_\eta>0$, $Y_t$ has a unit root.

With $\hat e_t$ the residuals from regressing $Y_t$ on a constant (or constant and trend) and partial sums $\hat S_t=\sum_{j=1}^{t}\hat e_j$:
$$
\text{KPSS}=\frac{1}{T^2\hat\lambda^2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat S_t^{\,2}.
$$

::: {.keybox}
Under stationarity the partial sums stay small; under a unit root they wander. **Right-tailed**: 5% critical values **0.463** (level) and **0.146** (trend).
:::

## Using both: confirmatory analysis {.smaller}

Unit-root tests have low power; stationarity tests over-reject for highly persistent stationary series. Neither is conclusive alone.

| | KPSS does not reject (stationary) | KPSS rejects |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **ADF/PP reject** (no unit root) | stationary — **consistent** | conflict: breaks, long memory or a near-unit root |
| **ADF/PP do not reject** | conflict: data uninformative, low power | unit root — **consistent** |

> **Predict:** for $Y_2$–$Y_5$ of the six-series exercise, which cell of this table should each series land in?

## R — ADF, PP and KPSS on $Y_2$–$Y_5$ {.smaller}

```{r}
tab <- rbind(`Y2 (level)` = confirm(y2, trend = FALSE),
             `Y3 (trend)` = confirm(y3, trend = TRUE),
             `Y4 (level)` = confirm(y4, trend = FALSE),
             `Y5 (trend)` = confirm(y5, trend = TRUE))
print(round(tab, 3))
verdict <- data.frame(`ADF rejects unit root`     = tab[, "ADF"]  < tab[, "ADF 5%"],
                      `PP rejects unit root`      = tab[, "PP"]   < tab[, "PP 5%"],
                      `KPSS rejects stationarity` = tab[, "KPSS"] > tab[, "KPSS 5%"],
                      check.names = FALSE)
cat("\n"); print(verdict)
```

::: {.small .muted}
`confirm()` (hidden setup chunk) runs `ur.df()` with BIC lags up to Schwert's $p_{\max}$, `ur.pp(type = "Z-tau")` and `ur.kpss()`, each with `lags = "short"` where relevant.
:::

## Reading the output {.smaller}

All four series land in **consistent** cells:

- $Y_2$ and $Y_3$: ADF and PP reject by a wide margin; KPSS (0.103 and 0.080) is far below its critical value — stationary around a **level** and around a **trend** respectively.
- $Y_4$ and $Y_5$: ADF and PP do not reject; KPSS rejects stationarity (3.996 and 0.605) — **unit roots**.

::: {.keybox}
With $T=500$ and no complications, the three tests agree. The Nelson–Plosser application shows a real series for which they do **not**.
:::

::: {.small .muted}
The ADF statistics differ slightly from the six-series slides because urca's BIC search always includes at least one lagged difference and drops the first $p_{\max}$ observations.
:::

## Size and power: the two notorious problems {.smaller}

- **Low power.** A stationary AR(1) with $\phi=0.95$ differs from a random walk only in the long run, and $T=100$ carries little information about the long run. Superfluous deterministic terms lower power further.
- **Size distortions.** When $\Delta Y_t$ has a large **negative** MA root (random walk plus noise; an over-differenced series), the MA root nearly cancels the AR unit root and tests reject a **true** unit root far too often (Schwert 1989).

::: {.keybox}
$$\boxed{\text{no rejection}\not\Rightarrow\text{unit root}}\ \text{(low power)}$$
$$\boxed{\text{rejection}\not\Rightarrow\text{no unit root}}\ \text{(negative MA roots)}$$
:::

## Practical lessons {.smaller}

1. **Span beats frequency.** Power depends on the length of time covered, not the number of observations: 30 years of monthly data carry little more information about mean reversion than 30 annual observations (Shiller and Perron 1985).
2. **Lag selection matters most when MA roots are large.** BIC tends to choose too few lags; AIC more; Ng and Perron's (2001) modified AIC was designed for this problem.
3. **Seasonality.** Seasonal dummies for deterministic seasonality; seasonal unit-root tests (Hylleberg, Engle, Granger and Yoo 1990) otherwise. Seasonal-adjustment filters can bias tests towards non-rejection (Ghysels and Perron 1993).
4. **Breaks** in the level or slope of a trend make a stationary series look like a unit root.

## Predict: a negative MA root {.smaller}

The true model is a random walk whose differences are MA(1),
$$
\Delta Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\beta\varepsilon_{t-1},\qquad \beta\in\{0,\,-0.5,\,-0.8\},\qquad T=100,
$$
so the unit-root null is **true**. All tests include a constant and have nominal size 5%; 1000 replications.

> **Predict:** how often will each reject?
>
> (a) DF without lags · (b) ADF, lags by BIC · (c) ADF, lags by AIC · (d) Phillips–Perron

## R — size with a negative MA root {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(123)
R <- 1000; T <- 100; betas <- c(0, -0.5, -0.8)
size <- sapply(betas, function(b) rowMeans(replicate(R, {
  y <- cumsum(as.numeric(arima.sim(model = list(ma = b), n = T)))
  c(`DF, no lags`     = df_tau(y, "drift") < -2.89,
    `ADF, BIC lags`   = adf_tau(y, "drift", pmax = 12, ic = "BIC")[["tau"]] < -2.89,
    `ADF, AIC lags`   = adf_tau(y, "drift", pmax = 12, ic = "AIC")[["tau"]] < -2.89,
    `Phillips-Perron` = { pp <- ur.pp(y, type = "Z-tau", model = "constant", lags = "short")
                          pp@teststat < pp@cval[1, "5pct"] })
})))
colnames(size) <- paste("beta =", betas)
cat("Rejection rates of a TRUE unit root, nominal size 5%:\n"); print(round(size, 3))
```

::: {.small .muted}
`adf_tau()` (hidden setup chunk) computes the ADF $t$-ratio with $p$ chosen by AIC or BIC over $0,\dots,p_{\max}$ on a common sample.
:::

## Reading the output {.smaller}

| | $\beta=0$ | $\beta=-0.5$ | $\beta=-0.8$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| DF, no lags | 0.049 | 0.561 | 0.996 |
| ADF, BIC lags | 0.045 | 0.202 | 0.696 |
| ADF, AIC lags | 0.065 | 0.131 | 0.452 |
| Phillips–Perron | 0.055 | 0.444 | 0.986 |

- With $\beta=0$ all four have about the right size (4.5–6.5%).
- With a negative MA root, DF without lags and PP reject the **true** unit root in most samples — virtually all at $\beta=-0.8$.
- Augmentation helps but does not cure it. **AIC beats BIC** because it picks longer lags, and long lags are needed to approximate an MA root near $-1$ by an autoregression.

::: {.keybox}
Don't rely on PP when the differences show strong negative autocorrelation; err on the **generous** side with ADF lags; prefer lag rules built for this case (Ng–Perron MAIC).
:::

## Appendix: R reference (1/2) {.smaller}

| Task | Function | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|
| (A)DF test | `urca::ur.df(y, type, lags, selectlags)` | `"none"/"drift"/"trend"`; with `"AIC"`/`"BIC"`, `lags` is the max and the search starts at 1 |
| Readable DF output | `df_report(y, type, lags, selectlags)` | this lecture's helper: regression, $\tau$/$\Phi$ vs 5% c.v., MacKinnon $p$ |
| MacKinnon $p$-values | `urca::punitroot(q, N, trend = "nc"/"c"/"ct")` | `qunitroot()` gives critical values for any $T$ |
| Phillips–Perron | `urca::ur.pp(y, type = "Z-tau", model, lags = "short"/"long")` | Newey–West bandwidth |
| KPSS | `urca::ur.kpss(y, type = "mu"/"tau", lags = "short"/"long")` | $H_0$: stationarity |
| DF-GLS, ERS $P_T$ | `urca::ur.ers(y, type = "DF-GLS"/"P-test", model, lag.max)` | GLS detrending |

## Appendix: R reference (2/2) {.smaller}

| Task | Function | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Zivot–Andrews | `urca::ur.za(y, model = "intercept"/"trend"/"both", lag)` | `@bpoint`: last period before the break |
| Schmidt–Phillips LM | `urca::ur.sp(y, type, pol.deg)` | LM test with polynomial trend |
| Quick ADF | `tseries::adf.test(y, k)` | always constant + trend; default `k = trunc((T-1)^(1/3))` |
| Explosive roots | `exuber::radf()`, `radf_mc_cv()`, `datestamp()` | SADF/GSADF and date-stamping |
| Number of differences | `forecast::ndiffs(y)`, `forecast::nsdiffs(y)` | KPSS-based (regular) and seasonal |
| ARIMA with drift | `arima(diff(y), order = c(p, 0, q))` or `forecast::Arima(y, order, include.drift = TRUE)` | `arima()` drops the constant when $d\ge1$ |
